messages.subject: Censored data problem
parts:
I have been trying to convert a (slightly adapted) example from the BUGS Book to Nimble, but I don't think it is working as it should.

The basic idea is that we are fitting a normal distribution with known variance to six observed data points, and we have three which are unobserved but we know are greater than eight.

This is the code I am using:

code <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:6) {y[i] ~ dnorm(mu, 1)}        # uncensored data

  ym[1]  ~ T(dnorm(mu,1), 8,)
  ym[2] ~ T(dnorm(mu,1), 8,)
  ym[3] ~  T(dnorm(mu,1), 8,)

  mu                   ~ dunif(0, 100)
})

data <- list(y = c(6,6,6,7,7,7), ym=c(NA,NA,NA))

inits <- list(mu = 7, ym = c(9,9,9))


mcmc.out <- nimbleMCMC(code = code,  data = data, inits = inits,  nchains = 2, niter = 100000, summary = TRUE, WAIC = TRUE,   monitors = c('mu', 'y', 'ym'))



However, what seems to be happening is that instead of finding the joint posterior of normal mean and three censored values, we are finding the posterior conditional only on the observed data, and imputing the censored values conditional on that (i.e., I would expect mu to be pulled up by the missing value estimates, but it is not):


> mcmc.out$summary$all.chains
          Mean   Median   St.Dev. 95%CI_low 95%CI_upp
mu    6.499750 6.499643 0.4060930  5.701948  7.295431
y[1]  6.000000 6.000000 0.0000000  6.000000  6.000000
y[2]  6.000000 6.000000 0.0000000  6.000000  6.000000
y[3]  6.000000 6.000000 0.0000000  6.000000  6.000000
y[4]  7.000000 7.000000 0.0000000  7.000000  7.000000
y[5]  7.000000 7.000000 0.0000000  7.000000  7.000000
y[6]  7.000000 7.000000 0.0000000  7.000000  7.000000
ym[1] 8.446887 8.335622 0.3989794  8.013438  9.482018
ym[2] 8.445184 8.333419 0.3980590  8.012746  9.477276
ym[3] 8.444607 8.335163 0.3958310  8.013012  9.471951



Any help here would be gratefully received.

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Censored data problem
parts:
Hi Rob, good question.

By setting the initial values of 'ym' to NA, NIMBLE actually treats
them as parameters and not as data.
Since there is not a known value, so there is no way to have NIMBLE
treat 'ym' as data in the way you are trying to do it.
As a result, NIMBLE sees the 'ym' elements as unknowns with no
children and simply simulates into them given the current value of mu
at any
given iteration.

What you need here is to make sure to include the likelihood
contribution from the three censored values. You can think of these
as being Bernoulli with probability equal to the probability of being
greater than 8. In reality the data you observe really are
indicators of those values being bigger than 8, so that is what needs
to be coded in the model.

So you should be able to do something like this:

for(i in 1:3)
ym[i] ~ dbern(pnorm(8, mu, 1, lower.tail = 0)) # note the
lower.tail argument needs to be numeric and not TRUE/FALSE
# alternatively: ym[i] ~ dbern(1-pnorm(8, mu, 1))

data = list(ym = rep(1, 3), .....)

Per table 5.2.5 of the NIMBLE manual, if you use distribution
functions in model code or nimbleFunctions, only some the canonical
parameterizations (essentially those that R uses) are allowed so the
"1" here is the standard deviation. See also Section 11.2.4 of the
manual.

I haven't had the time to look more carefully at what BUGS and JAGS
would do in this case, but we modeled NIMBLE's handling of truncation
off of
what JAGS does, so I believe how one handles this in JAGS would be
along the lines of what I have above. But I could be wrong.

If anyone reading wants to weigh in on the comparison with BUGS and
JAGS for this sort of situation, please do!

-chris
